opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that there's a real tension at the heart of it. Effective altruism grew up around things you *could* measure: GiveWell's early work on bed nets, deworming, cash transfers. The whole culture came from "let's look at the randomized controlled trials, let's estimate cost per life saved, let's be rigorous." That's a really powerful instinct, and it's done a lot of good.

But as the community, and Open Philanthropy in particular, moved into areas like AI safety, biosecurity, or speculative long-term work, you run into questions where there's no RCT and never will be. You can't run a trial on "how likely is transformative AI by 2040" or "does this research agenda reduce catastrophic risk."

So what characterizes the approach, at its best, is trying to keep the *spirit* of rigor when the *letter* of it isn't available. That means making your reasoning explicit: writing down your assumptions, putting rough numbers on things even when they're very uncertain, and showing your work so other people can see exactly where they disagree with you. My biological anchors report was very much in that vein. I didn't think it gave the answer to when transformative AI would arrive. It was a way to structure the question so that disagreements became legible. Is it about how much compute the brain uses? About algorithmic progress? About how much people will spend?

There's also a heavy emphasis on things like calibration, forecasting, and worldview diversification, the idea that if you're deeply uncertain between frameworks, you shouldn't put everything on one of them.

The failure mode, and I think it's real, is false precision. You write down a number like "10% chance" and it starts to feel more solid than it is, or a long chain of guesstimates takes on authority it hasn't earned. The opposite failure mode is giving up and going purely on vibes. I'd say the culture is constantly trying to walk between those two, and doesn't always succeed, but I think the commitment to explicit, criticizable reasoning is the right core instinct.

r002.rationale: It describes making explicit estimates and assumptions on difficult questions, while showing where others may disagree and acknowledging uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's distinctive about the EA approach, and I'd include Open Philanthropy where I used to work in this, is that when a question resists rigorous measurement, the instinct isn't to throw up your hands and say "well, that's just a matter of values" or "we can't know." The instinct is to try to quantify anyway, while being really explicit that the quantification is rough.

So the classic version of this is GiveWell. If you're comparing bednets to deworming to cash transfers, those have pretty different outcome measures, and you have to make some kind of judgment call about how to trade off a death averted against an income increase. GiveWell's move was to say, okay, we're going to write down a number for that tradeoff, and we're going to show our work, and we're going to argue about it in public, and we know the number is partly made up. But a number that's partly made up and open to critique beats a vibe that's entirely made up and hidden.

And then when you get to the stuff I spent most of my time on, like timelines to transformative AI, it's the same spirit pushed much further. There is no dataset you can run a regression on. So you build a model with a bunch of explicit assumptions, you put probability distributions on the inputs rather than point estimates, and you treat the output as a way of structuring the disagreement rather than as the answer. The real value of the biological anchors report, in my view, wasn't the median year. It was that people who disagreed with me could point to a specific parameter and say "I think that's off by an order of magnitude," and then we could have a conversation about that instead of just trading intuitions.

I'd also say there's a strong norm of reasoning transparency. You try to say not just what you believe but how confident you are, what would change your mind, and where the weak links are. And there's a willingness to act on best guesses under uncertainty rather than waiting for certainty that's never coming.

Now, the failure modes are real. You can get false precision, where a number acquires authority just because it's a number. You can end up anchoring everyone on one model because it's the only one that exists. And there's a selection effect where the things that are easiest to model get the most attention. I think the community is reasonably self-aware about that, but it's a constant pull. So I'd describe the approach as: quantify anyway, be honest that it's rough, make it legible enough to argue with, and keep updating.

r001.rationale: The response says GiveWell must make a judgment call about trading off a death averted against an income increase when comparing interventions.

r002.rationale: It describes EA’s instinct as quantifying difficult questions despite roughness, making assumptions explicit, and keeping answers open to public critique.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing that characterizes a lot of effective altruism organizations is a willingness to try to reason explicitly about questions even when we can’t measure the answers very well. So rather than saying, “This is too speculative to analyze,” you ask, “What do we believe? Why do we believe it? What would change our minds?”

That might involve putting numbers on things, but ideally those numbers are a way of making your uncertainty legible, rather than claiming a level of precision you don’t actually have. If you’re making a decision, you’re implicitly making some judgment about which option is better. Writing down your assumptions gives other people a chance to challenge that judgment.

And I think there’s a real tension there. You want the discipline of explicit reasoning, but you don’t want the fact that something fits neatly into a spreadsheet to give it more weight than it deserves. A lot of the hard work is figuring out which considerations your model is leaving out, and how much those should affect the decision.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention GiveWell or compare income gains with health outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says EA organizations are willing to reason explicitly about questions that are hard to measure, and notes that assumptions and judgments remain open to challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing that characterizes a lot of effective altruism organizations is a willingness to try to reason explicitly about those questions, even when you can’t measure the answer very well. You can say, “Here are the things we’re uncertain about. Here’s why we currently favor this option. What would have to be true for another option to look better?”

And sometimes putting numbers on things helps clarify that reasoning. But I don’t think the number itself makes the judgment rigorous. You can have a spreadsheet that’s mostly encoding intuitions, and it’s important to recognize that. The value is in making those intuitions and assumptions visible enough that other people can challenge them, and that you can update as you learn more.
